title: Reference Check from Hell
tagline: Recommend the ruin. Seal the fate.
premise: Three rounds. Each round deals one job nobody wants, described by a dull fact about its work. Both players write one sentence from a former boss recommending the applicant. The work must remain recognisable, and the sentence must still make the applicant suitable and willing to do it. Everything else is fair game: grudges, secret talents, warnings, crimes, romance, bodily fluids and the precise reason nobody else applied. The Host scores how strangely the reference recommends the doomed applicant while the job still stands.

seed_pool.opening_token: Stand outside a nightclub and hold umbrellas for strangers in the rain.
Count escaped chickens at a farm gate.
Clean the changing rooms after a wrestling tournament.

task: guard a pile of wet coats
sort socks from a lost property bin

tests: One plain sentence, past or present tense, under fifteen words. A stranger sees the job at once.
Nobody is murdered, seriously injured or forced into sexual activity. The misery is comic and workplace-sized.
It describes work a person could actually be hired to do, however vile, pointless or socially cursed.
It contains a setting and a task, with at least one noun a reference can turn into a witness, weapon or scandal.
It names one checkable ordeal, such as rain, a time, a number or a missing object, that a reference can keep or twist without erasing.

move_constraints.example: Reliable, discreet, and has never asked what was in the bin.
move_constraints.hint: One reference sentence. Recommend the applicant, then reveal why the job should terrify us.

rubric.name: stretch
rubric.description: How far does the reference turn a grim little job into a personal catastrophe while still recommending the applicant for it?
rubric.anchors: 0 = repeats the job with no angle; 1 = adds one mild compliment; 2 = gives a strange skill, motive or warning; 3 = invents a full history of disgrace, danger or devotion while the applicant still suits the job; 4 = a devastating character reference that makes the vacancy feel like evidence in a trial, yet still recommends the applicant without blinking (rare).

rubric.name: funny
rubric.description: Does the former boss's praise create a clean comic hit?
rubric.anchors: 0 = flat; 1 = a small twitch; 2 = a smile at the applicant's expense; 3 = a proper laugh; 4 = a sentence the room repeats because the recommendation is worse than the job (rare). Grim sincerity usually beats a wink.

rubric.name: headline_shaped
rubric.description: Does it work as one crisp reference sentence, with praise doing the damage?
rubric.anchors: 0 = not a reference, an explanation or a paragraph; 1 = a recommendation buried under padding; 2 = recognisable but loose; 3 = compact, grammatical and clearly from a former boss; 4 = every word sounds useful until the final implication arrives (rare).

criterion.description: A reference PLAYS if a reader who knows only the reference can still understand that the applicant is suitable and willing to perform the card's stated job. The job may be made filthy, sinister, humiliating or absurd, but it must remain the job. The sentence fails when it drops the work entirely, makes the applicant unwilling or unsuitable, replaces the task with another one, or becomes a comment about the game rather than a reference. A plain recommendation that merely repeats the card plays and scores near zero on stretch.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Host, discussing the round or explaining the scoring is not a reference and loses the move.
judge_notes:
Test the first move by asking whether a stranger can identify both the work and the applicant's willingness to do it. "Punctual, fearless, and already knows every chicken by its alias" passes for counting escaped chickens because the task remains clear and the applicant sounds ready.
Dropping the job fails. "A troubled soul who should never be left alone with a clipboard" is not enough for holding umbrellas outside a nightclub because no work survives.
Refusing the work fails. "Brilliant, but she will not stand in the rain" contradicts a job requiring the applicant to stand in the rain.
Unsuitability fails. "A perfect umbrella holder, provided he is never near an umbrella" breaks the stated task rather than recommending the applicant for it.
Replacing the task fails. "He would make an excellent bouncer" does not recommend someone to hold umbrellas, even if a nightclub appears in the card.
Invented detail is allowed when it supports the recommendation. A criminal record, a secret romance, a vendetta against poultry or a disturbing level of stamina may all play if the applicant still does the stated work.
Both players answer the same card. Judge each reference on its own; the other player's sentence is not the standard.
Score stretch by distance from the job, not by cruelty alone. A surgical reference that turns umbrella duty into a rain soaked custody dispute beats a loud insult with no work in it.
Lower case, capitals, a missing full stop and ordinary spelling do not matter. The words and their meaning do.

voice_rules: One sentence under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Speak as though stamping a formal document while observing a preventable disaster.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who saw only the card and the reference must understand the recommendation and the damage.
Name the job's key object or task, the umbrella, the chicken, the mop, the wet coat. Generic praise is a vacant form.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No "Accepted", "Rejected", "Refused", "The Registrar refuses".
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Roast the reference and its applicant, not identity groups or protected traits. A little adult innuendo and profanity are permitted when the sentence earns them.
Plain spoken English. Ceremonial does not mean flowery. No legal fog, no HR jargon, no fake Latin.
On a fail, state the exact work that vanished, was refused or got replaced, using the card's own words.
On a refusal, the gate failure rejects the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one reference that would have passed. It ends on a job, an object or an action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The umbrella duty remains, and so does the unexplained moisture in the applicant's file.
The chickens are counted, the alias is known, and the farm has accepted its new intelligence officer.
The changing rooms are clean, though calling him The Final Witness has not helped recruitment.
This is a reference for umbrella holding, not a confession, though the distinction is failing.
The applicant still counts chickens, and apparently counts them as people with grudges.
A wet coat was required, and the reference has supplied one with a criminal history.
The job is still cleaning wrestling rooms. The sentence merely makes the mop look complicit.
The applicant refuses wet fabric, so the umbrella job has lost its only employee.
Nightclub security is not umbrella duty, however confidently the applicant's career is redirected.
The chicken count disappeared beneath the leadership speech. Put the gate and the poultry back in.

rules: Three rounds, one unwanted job each.
Write one reference sentence for it, under 90 characters. The House writes its own, unseen, and the Registrar scores both.
The reference must still recommend an applicant suitable and willing to do the stated job. Drop, refuse or replace the work and the round is lost.
Everything else is yours to invent. The stranger the recommendation while the job survives, the more you score. Most points after three rounds wins.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your reference while you wait

validation_messages.too_long: Over 90 characters. A reference, not a memoir.
validation_messages.duplicate: That reference has already been filed this match. Find another stain.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. One reference that keeps this job alive: {standing_form}.

judge_out_text: The Registrar has stepped away to locate the personnel file. Nobody is hired until they return. {standing_form} remains unsigned. Give it a moment.
opponent_prompt:
You are a former boss writing one reference sentence for a job nobody wants. Write one
sentence under 90 characters.
THE JOB MUST SURVIVE. A reader who sees only your reference must still understand that the
applicant is suitable and willing to do the stated work. Never drop the task, refuse it,
or replace it with another career.
Then go as far as you dare. Invent the applicant's history, secret talent, grievance,
crime, romance, bodily problem or terrifying dedication. The points are for distance from
the dull job while the recommendation still holds.
Good: "Punctual, fearless, and already knows every chicken by its alias" for counting
escaped chickens. "Discreet, steady, and never asks why the coats are warm" for guarding
wet coats. "A superb cleaner, though the wrestlers still call him The Final Witness" for
cleaning changing rooms.
Bad: "A fascinating person" because the work vanished. "He refuses to stand in the rain"
because the applicant is unwilling. "Excellent bouncer" because the task was replaced.
Use one crisp reference sentence. Praise should do the damage. Under 90 characters. Do not
use a colon or a dash. Do not explain the joke. Capitals are fine but not required.
Vary the angle from round to round: a warning, a secret talent, a suspicious compliment,
a past incident, a cost saving or a private feud. Never the same shape twice in a match.
No quotation marks around the reference. Reply with the reference only.
default_move: Reliable, discreet, and willing to do the job nobody else would touch
